sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Brown Syndrome is a restrictive ocular motility disorder where the eyeball is mechanically prevented from moving upward when it is turned toward the nose (adduction). It is primarily caused by an abnormality of the Superior Oblique (SO) tendon-trochlea complex, preventing the smooth passage of the tendon through the trochlear pulley.

branches: Acquired: Iatrogenic (Following SO tuck or scleral buckling)

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Deficient elevation in adduction (Primary Sign).
Normal or near-normal elevation in abduction.
Down-shoot of the eye in adduction.
V-pattern exotropia (divergence in up-gaze).
Compensatory head posture (Chin-up and contralateral head tilt).
Positive 'click' or 'snap' felt by the patient in intermittent cases.
Widening of the palpebral fissure on adduction.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Brown vs. IO Palsy
Forced Duction Test (FDT) Protocol
content: Step 1: Instill topical proparacaine or perform under general anesthesia.
Step 2: Grasp the globe at the limbus (usually 6 o'clock and 12 o'clock).
Step 3: Attempt to move the globe into elevation while in the adducted position.
Step 4: Assess for mechanical resistance. In Brown, there is a hard stop.
Step 5: Compare resistance in abduction (should be free).

sections.title: Wright's Grading System
content: Mild: Restricted elevation in adduction; no hypotropia or downshoot in primary position.
Moderate: Restricted elevation in adduction + downshoot in adduction; no hypotropia in primary.
Severe: Marked restriction in elevation in adduction + marked downshoot + hypotropia in primary position.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Hess Chart/Lees Screen: Shows constricted field of elevation in adduction.
High-Resolution MRI (Orbits): To visualize SO tendon thickening or trochlear inflammation.
Blood Work: ESR, CRP, RF, and Anti-CCP if inflammatory etiology is suspected.
Prism Cover Test: In 9 cardinal positions of gaze.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Diagnosis: Confirm mechanical restriction via FDT.
Conservative: Observation if no primary position deviation or abnormal head posture.
Medical: Local corticosteroid injection to the trochlear area (for acquired inflammatory cases).
Medical: Systemic NSAIDs for painful 'clicking' cases.
Surgery: Indicated for significant hypotropia in primary position or severe head tilt.
Post-Op: Immediate aggressive duction exercises to prevent adhesion.

rows: Risk of creating SO palsy; unpredictable.
Maintains tendon direction; reduces SO palsy risk; may extrude or cause granuloma.
Adjustable but can lead to scarring/adhesion.

sections.title: Red Flags & Urgent Considerations
content: Rapid onset of painful motility restriction (Suspect Orbital Myositis).
New onset head tilt in adults (Rule out underlying systemic disease).
Associated Proptosis or Vision Loss (Suspect Neoplasm/Apex Syndrome).
Failure of FDT to show restriction (Re-evaluate for IO Palsy or CN III palsy).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Prep
content: Brown syndrome is 'elevation deficiency in adduction' - remember the SO tendon is too short to allow the eye to go up and in.
The 'True' Brown syndrome is ALWAYS restrictive on FDT.
Simulated Brown Syndrome: Can occur after a scleral buckle or orbital roof fracture.
Surgical overcorrection is common; patients may end up with a Superior Oblique Palsy.

content.explanation: B: Below (Hypotropia in adduction), R: Restrictive FDT, O: Oblique (SO) tendon issue, W: Widening of fissure on adduction, N: Normal elevation in abduction.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Landmark Insights
sections.content: Recent studies using high-resolution dynamic MRI have shown that some cases of 'congenital' Brown are actually associated with SO tendon hypoplasia or abnormal pulleys. Additionally, the use of non-absorbable 'Chicken-beak' silicone expanders (Wright's technique) remains the gold standard for reducing the high rate of iatrogenic SO palsy seen with simple tenotomy.

sections.content: Brown syndrome is a restrictive motility disorder characterized by the inability to elevate the eye in adduction. This comprehensive guide covers the mechanical pathophysiology of the trochlear-tendon complex, diagnostic pearls, and the surgical nuances of tendon lengthening.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Brown syndrome (Superior Oblique Tendon Sheath Syndrome) is a mechanical restriction of the superior oblique (SO) tendon's movement through the trochlea. Pathophysiology involves a short or inelastic SO tendon, or an inflammatory thickening (nodule) that prevents the tendon from sliding through the pulley mechanism when the eye attempts to elevate in an adducted position.

sections.title: Clinical Hallmarks: The Diagnostic Triad
content: Severe limitation of elevation in ADDUCTION.
Minimal or no limitation of elevation in ABDUCTION.
Minimal or no Superior Oblique Overaction (SOOA) — helps distinguish from IO Palsy.
Positive Forced Duction Test (FDT) on attempt to elevate the eye in adduction.
V-pattern strabismus (divergence in upgaze).
Downshoot in adduction (pseudo-overaction of the SO).

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Brown vs. IO Palsy

rows: Limited elevation in adduction; No downshoot; Ortho in primary.
Limited elevation in adduction; Downshoot in adduction; Ortho in primary.
Severe limitation in adduction; Marked downshoot; Hypotropia in primary.

sections.title: The Forced Duction Test (FDT) Protocol
content: Step 1: Instill topical anesthetic (proparacaine) or perform under general anesthesia.
Step 2: Grasp the limbus at 3 and 9 o'clock with toothed forceps.
Step 3: Move the globe into an adducted position.
Step 4: Attempt to rotate the globe upward (elevation).
Step 5: Feel for mechanical resistance (positive result if eye cannot be elevated).

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Observation for asymptomatic patients with good binocular vision/no head tilt.
Step 2: Treat underlying inflammation (Steroids/NSAIDS) for acquired/inflammatory cases.
Step 3: Steroid injection (Triamcinolone 40mg) near the trochlea for 'Click Syndrome'.
Step 4: Surgical Intervention if there is hypotropia in primary position or significant abnormal head tilt.
Step 5: Post-operative monitoring for Inferior Oblique Overaction (consecutive palsy).

sections.title: Surgical Techniques & Options
content: SO Tenotomy or Tenectomy: Simple but high risk of SO palsy.
SO Tendon Lengthening: Using a silicone spacer (Wright's technique).
SO Tendon Suture Spacers (Non-absorbable): Graduated lengthening.
Split-Tendon Lengthening: Z-plasty of the tendon.
Superior Oblique Recession: Less effective due to anatomical constraints.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Acquired Brown
content: Sudden onset in adulthood
Pain upon eye movement or palpation of the trochlea
History of Rheumatoid Arthritis or Autoimmune disease
Recent orbital trauma or sinus surgery
Intermittent 'locking' and 'unlocking' with an audible click

content.explanation: B: Below (Hypotropia in primary if severe); R: Restriction on FDT; O: Outward (V-pattern divergence); W: Worse in adduction; N: No SO overaction.

sections.title: Canine Tooth Syndrome
sections.content: A specific subset of traumatic Brown syndrome caused by penetrating injury to the trochlea (classically a dog bite to the superior medial orbit). It results in a combined Brown syndrome and Superior Oblique palsy due to damage to both the trochlea and the nerve/muscle fibers.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Acquired Brown syndrome is more likely to resolve spontaneously than congenital.
The 'Click' in intermittent Brown syndrome represents the nodule snapping through the trochlea.
A compensatory chin-up and contralateral head tilt are common to maintain binocularity.
In surgical spacers, the standard length of silicone used is 6mm to 7mm.
Always check for IO palsy in the DDx using the Parks 3-step test (though 3-step is for paretic, not restrictive).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Recent Advances
content: The Wright Silicone Spacer Study: Established the use of medical-grade silicone for controlled tendon lengthening to prevent consecutive SO palsy.
MRI Studies: Demonstrated that in some 'True' Brown cases, the SO muscle belly is actually hypoplastic.
Bupivacaine Injection: Emerging research into chemodenervation/activation, though not yet standard of care.
Botulinum Toxin: Limited utility in Brown, but occasionally used in the SO for acute inflammatory phases.

sections.title: Complications of Surgery
content: Consecutive Superior Oblique Palsy (Most common)
Extrusion of the silicone spacer (Foreign body reaction)
Persistence of restriction (Under-correction)
Fat Adherence Syndrome
Post-operative scarring/Adhesions

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging Workup
content: Thin-cut MRI of the Orbits (Coronal & Sagittal views).
Focus on the trochlea and SO tendon complex.
Look for: Tendon thickening, enhancement (inflammatory), or trochlear masses.
Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM): Can sometimes visualize the anterior tendon dynamics.
